results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 67 aligned outline summaries are fair short paraphrases of their spec paragraphs' controlling ideas, in spec order (including the goes-wrong order p59, p60, p58). The three introduction callouts map to the thesis_statement/roadmap placements, not to a paragraph, and are left unmatched.

The only unit marked two_ideas is What to Take Away ¶4 (p65, 'The author's synthesis'), a labelled two-bullet list. Its controlling idea is the author's own judgement, of which the two bullets are the items, the same list form as the sibling units p63 and p64 that the outliner did not flag; the spec's p65 deliberately names both items. Accepted as one idea with its items.
Every body unit supports S1-S5 as its section's advances_thesis declares; introduction, transition (p36, p55) and conclusion units trace by role.

Each table (dimensions, components, per-flow, trade-offs, stages, the jacket on 13 April), each figure (captions say what it shows) and each quotation (98/6/EC, Article 6a, SAP KBA, Google, ACM) has a sentence saying what it shows. The Shopify limit's relation to Kestrel & Pine's four B2B lists is a flow problem, ruled under flow_is_followable.

Every declared transition_in is expressed at its boundary (e.g. 'Eleven prices for one jacket are not in themselves the fault', 'The rule, the moment, the dated history and the channel rules each need a place to live', 'The components say what must exist', 'The last failure is of a different kind'), the conclusion's phrase labels carry p63-p65, and the last paragraph hands off to [[commerce-promotions]] with the frozen price carried over.

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: The Price Drift ¶6
results.quote: One jacket, eleven prices, seven places, no rule saying which was the source of which.
results.finding: Neither reader can reconstruct eleven prices or seven places from the inventory just given (they count four to six places and more or fewer than eleven prices); the bold count is the scene's punchline and is reused later ('A merchant whose prices live in seven places'). The inventory should enumerate the seven places and the eleven prices so they add up.

results.draft_locus: Tax, Markets and Currencies: Why €199 Is Three Different Prices (heading)
results.quote: Tax, Markets and Currencies: Why €199 Is Three Different Prices
results.finding: Both readers looked for the third price and did not find it: the section shows two net amounts (€164.46 for NL and BE, €167.23 for DE). Either name the three amounts the heading means or reword the heading.

results.draft_locus: The Price Rules Europe Writes Into the System ¶1
results.quote: Their dates matter, because "we did not know" is the Long Fuse.
results.finding: The failure-pattern name is known from Part I, but used this compressed it stops both readers at the start of the section: they had to guess what the Long Fuse is and why not knowing the dates is an instance of it. One clause saying what the Long Fuse is (a legal exposure that goes off long after its cause) would fix it.

results.quote: The shop platform already held Kestrel & Pine's three market and four B2B lists, so that assumption held.
results.finding: The sentence declares the first assumption held right after quoting Shopify's 'up to 3 active catalog assignments' below Plus, while Kestrel & Pine has four B2B lists, and it checks only list capacity, not the price history that is half the assumption and that the Black Friday test relies on. Reader B also had to scroll back to recall the assumptions because the stage section sits between them and their check (an order the spec chose deliberately, so the fix is in the prose: restate the assumption in full and say how the limit and the history apply to Kestrel & Pine).

results.quote: [[product-information]] gave every product attribute one owner and left the price out of that table.
results.finding: Both readers found the bridge from the previous chapter out of place between the prescription ('Assign an owner to the rule ... drift as soon as one changes') and the journey box, and both propose moving it to the start of the opening prose or next to the roadmap. The draft follows the spec's order p01, p02, p03, so the order is the spec's. Both rate it a small hitch.

results.draft_locus: Across Scale Stages: When It Fits and When It Limits ¶2
results.quote: The source decision changes at the Growing stage, when the ERP arrives and the merchant must say which prices it owns, and again only at the Group stage, if several brands share a pricing service; between the two the work is in the copies.
results.finding: Reader A stopped here: Kestrel & Pine is at the Omnichannel stage and its 2027 design changes the source decision (consumer prices leave the ERP), which seems to contradict 'again only at the Group stage ... between the two the work is in the copies'. The judgement needs a clause reconciling it with the case (e.g. that Kestrel & Pine is correcting a Growing-stage decision it never made).

results.quote: The examples in the last column come from the design Kestrel & Pine adopted in 2027; the sections that follow argue for it.
results.finding: Reader A: the components table shows the outcome (consumer lists in the shop platform, wholesale and contract lists in the ERP) before The Choices and Trade-offs argue for it, so the argument reads backwards. The draft flags this as the spec's p29 requires, so the cause is the spec's choice of examples; the reader says it is not confusing, only backwards.

results.draft_locus: The Price Rules Europe Writes Into the System ¶4
results.quote: On 5 February 2026 the Bundeskartellamt, Germany's competition authority, prohibited a different control: Amazon's own **price control mechanisms**, which removed or hid offers it judged too expensive
results.finding: Reader A could not tell whether the PRICING_HEALTH / Buy Box notification described next is the mechanism prohibited in Germany or something still allowed, nor how the 2026 parity warning in the Price Drift squares with parity clauses deleted in 2013. One sentence saying what is still allowed would settle it.

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: The Price Drift ¶6
results.quote: The ERP held the wholesale and contract prices again, for invoicing, and the consumer lists that fed the DE storefront and the POS file.
results.finding: Reader B had to re-read to work out whether the shop platform's DE market list (named in the same paragraph) was a copy of the ERP's German consumer list or a separate list; the paragraph lists holdings without saying which fed which.

results.draft_locus: Tax, Markets and Currencies: Why €199 Is Three Different Prices ¶3
results.quote: The alternative, one net price with the gross (VAT-inclusive) price derived, would give the shopper €199.00 in Nijmegen and €195.71 in Munich
results.finding: Reader B had to do the arithmetic to see that the one net price is the Dutch net €164.46 grossed up at 19%; the sentence should name which net price is used.

Both readers describe the organising principle as problem, vocabulary, constraints, architecture, options, test, failures, which agrees with the declared prerequisite_order with problem_solution, comparison and grouping sub-patterns; no section's position is unclear to either. Material lost-thread points are failed above. Four trivial points left out: reader A point 3 (bold vocabulary 'is the chapter's'), reader A point 10 ('idempotent', known from Part I), reader B point 5 (rounding pointer to the next section), reader B point 7 (Waypoint W5, known from Part I).

results.quote: below the Plus plan allows "up to 3 active catalog assignments across active B2B markets"
results.finding: 'Catalog assignment' (and the Plus plan) are never explained, so a newcomer cannot tell whether the limit applies to Kestrel & Pine's four B2B lists; this is the term behind the flow readers' confusion about whether catalogs and B2B lists are the same thing.

results.quote: commercetools allows up to 100 embedded prices per variant or 50,000 standalone prices
results.finding: 'Embedded' versus 'standalone' prices is never explained (standalone appears earlier only as commercetools' name for a price list), so a reader new to commerce cannot read the limit.

Other terms in terms.txt are acceptable for this audience: market, customer group, validity, deterministic, engine and copies, repricer and price list appear first in the summary callouts or in plain-English use and are defined soon after; contract price is defined two paragraphs after its first use in the inventory; margin, dynamic rules and deduction are plain business words or explained in place; Bergzicht, Waypoint and the failure-pattern names come from Part I; vendor names (commercetools, SAP Commerce, Adobe Commerce, Google Merchant Center) are identified by context as platforms or feed specifications; Europe1 and Javadoc appear only in citations.
Opens on an intriguing example (€199 vs €95 for one jacket), then the claim, the bridge from product-information, Eva's order and a roadmap; no weak pattern.

Opens with the callback and a synthesis, then labelled Established / Depends on context / author's synthesis lists, questions and a hand-off; the Established list restates sources as the spec's p63 asks, not new body evidence.

States what no section states alone ('The remedy and the legal duty need the same record ... ends a campaign without a restoring message, gives the daily comparison something to compare ... and answers the 30-day question') and why it matters ('can explain every price it shows, to a customer, a marketplace or a regulator'). The spec's contrast half of so_what (a merchant typing prices into each system finds out from a marketplace warning or margin report) is not stated, but the substance is there.
'The chapter opened with one jacket at €199 for a consumer and €95 for a wholesale buyer. Both prices are right, because each has a source and a rule that selects it.'

The intro reader lists the sections in the spec's order (Price Drift, what a price is made of and the rule, tax/markets/currencies, European rules, engine vs copies and who may change a price, four arrangements with trade-offs and stages, platform documentation and the 2027 design, how pricing fails) and the evidence (the Price Drift, EU legal requirements, platform documentation).

The answer names the silent restore (restore update lost, reported as success, never retried), a daily reconciliation of every copy against its source as the next-morning detection, and the 2027 single dated campaign row that needs no restore message; it does not propose pushing more often.

The answer says the post-campaign €199 is charged, selected once at order placement by the same rule and data as the storefront, frozen on the order, and that the invoice copies it and never recomputes.

The answer gives the lowest price for that SKU in that market in the previous 30 days, from an effective-dated price history, because Directive 2019/2161 (Article 6a) requires an announced reduction to show it.

The answer gives the split by kind (consumer prices and campaigns in the shop platform, wholesale and contract in the ERP, other systems fed by dated events and compared daily), the three assumptions, and a pricing service when one assumption fails or with many markets, currencies, groups or storefronts.
